001: Seinfeld was the massively popular 1990s NBC sitcom about four self-absorbed friends in New York, famously self-described as 'a show about nothing.' Its characters, who fuss obsessively over trivia while shrugging off morality, turn out to be ideal test cases for serious questions: Can George ever become virtuous, or is he doomed by habit? Is Elaine a feminist icon? Is Kramer Kierkegaard's aesthete, fleeing commitment in an endless rotation of schemes? Even the show's 'nothing' becomes a question about whether nothingness can be something.
003: The Matrix (1999) is the landmark science-fiction film in which hacker Neo discovers that ordinary life is a computer simulation fed to humans whose bodies power the machines. The red pill/blue pill choice made it the perfect hook for philosophy: How do you know you are not deceived, right now? The essays here read Neo as Socrates waking up Athens, his unplugging as Plato's cave allegory, and the film as a Rorschach blot in which skeptics, Christians, and Buddhists alike can find their questions.
004: Buffy the Vampire Slayer (1997-2003) is Joss Whedon’s television series about a teenage girl chosen to hunt vampires in the ordinary California town of Sunnydale, and it became one of the most studied shows in television for the way it fused genre adventure with real moral weight. Behind the demons, the show is about growing up: friendship, love and sex, death, autonomy, and the cost of duty — questions the essays here read through Sartre, Kant, Aristotle, and feminism. Its high-school metaphor (hell literally under the school) made it a natural meeting point between philosophy and popular storytelling.
005: The Lord of the Rings is Tolkien's monumental 1950s fantasy epic of hobbits, wizards, and a quest to destroy a ring of absolute power, beloved worldwide and famously filmed by Peter Jackson. Its central device is a philosophical thought experiment: Plato's Ring of Gyges, which grants impunity. Would anyone remain just? From Gollum to Galadriel to Frodo at the Crack of Doom, Tolkien dramatizes how unlimited power corrupts. The essays also mine Middle-earth for answers on happiness, friendship, fetishism, and joy amid sorrow.
006: Baseball, America's old pastoral ballgame of bats, bases, and endless statistics, has generated more argument than any other sport, which makes it fertile philosophical ground. What does it mean to sacrifice with a bunt? Is rooting for the perpetually losing Cubs a form of religious faith? Do the rules themselves contain contradictions? The essays here weigh cheating and sportsmanship through Kant and Aristotle, umpire discretion through Austin and Dworkin, and even what the ballpark's 'home' says about belonging.
007: The Sopranos (1999-2007) is the celebrated HBO drama about Tony Soprano, a New Jersey mob boss who begins seeing a therapist while running a criminal family alongside his real one. It invites philosophy because it is an existential drama disguised as a gangster story: why does a man with everything feel like a loser? Can Tony's code of honor survive his own appetites? Is he a Machiavellian prince, a Nietzschean nihilist sunk in resentment, or just an 'ethical manager' of a murderous business?
008: Woody Allen is the American filmmaker and comedian whose anxious, joke-laden films of the 1970s through 1990s, from Annie Hall to Crimes and Misdemeanors, made neurosis and moral panic entertaining. His characters are philosophy generators: If nothing in the universe is permanent, can life have meaning? Is integrity more than consistency? Can Judah murder and get away with it in a world without God? The essays take his comedies seriously as arguments about despair, faith, hedonism, and how to appreciate art.
009: Harry Potter is J.K. Rowling's seven-novel fantasy series (1997-2007) about a boy wizard at Hogwarts school, the best-selling book series in history. Rowling, like Tolkien and Lewis, poses real philosophical problems for young readers: What is a soul, and can Voldemort's Horcruxes really split one? Does prophecy, such as the one marking Harry as the Chosen One, leave any room for free choice? Is love the most powerful magic? The essays test the wizarding world against ancient and modern theories of mind, identity, and destiny.
010: The Passion of the Christ (2004) is Mel Gibson's brutally graphic film of Jesus's final twelve hours, one of the highest-grossing religious films ever made and an instant lightning rod for controversy. Because its subject is God incarnate suffering, its questions cut deeper than most movie philosophy: Why did Christ have to die so violently, and what does atonement mean? Is the film anti-Semitic? Can Judas be blamed for a betrayal God foreknew? Is the gore a route to the sublime or a distortion of the whole person?
012: Star Wars is George Lucas's epoch-making space-fantasy saga (from 1977) of the Skywalker family, the evil Empire, and the mystical Force, one of the most beloved film series ever made. Its black-and-white conflict hides surprisingly rich questions: Are Anakin and Luke really free if a prophecy foretold their fates? Is Yoda a Stoic sage, and the Jedi path a kind of Zen? Is Lando's betrayal of Han a defensible utilitarian choice? The essays trace virtue, evil, and destiny through a galaxy far, far away.
013: Superman, Batman, and Spider-Man began as comic-book characters in the 1930s and 1960s and have since become worldwide icons through blockbuster films. Superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, work as modern myths that dramatize philosophy's deepest questions: what makes someone a hero, whether an invulnerable being can risk anything, when crime-fighting becomes vigilantism, and how selflessness relates to self-interest. Philosophers and comic-book writers tackle them together, from Plato and Aristotle to Watchmen's question of who watches the watchmen.
014: The Atkins Diet is the low-carbohydrate regimen first popularized by Dr. Robert Atkins in the 1970s, which tells dieters to skip bread and sugar and eat meat and fat instead, defying mainstream nutrition advice while selling millions of books. Precisely because it flouts expert consensus, it raises genuine philosophical puzzles: how should a rational person decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe? Essays draw on Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, and Dewey to examine habit, autonomy, low-carb nostalgia for a hunter-gatherer past, and the quality of the evidence in diet books.
015: The Chronicles of Narnia is C.S. Lewis's beloved seven-book fantasy series (1950-1956), in which English children pass through a wardrobe and other doorways into a magical land ruled by the lion Aslan. Lewis taught philosophy at Oxford before becoming Christianity's best-known modern apologist, and his stories quietly stage serious questions: when should you believe incredible testimony, what may be accepted on faith, could more than one religion be true, and could a boy turned into a dragon remain the same person? Philosophers work through them with epistemology, Hume, Kierkegaard, and Pascal.
016: Hip-hop is the culture born in the 1970s Bronx - rapping, DJing, breakdancing, and graffiti - now a dominant force in popular music worldwide. This book takes seriously hip-hop's self-declared but often suppressed fifth element, knowledge, treating MCs like Rakim, Lauryn Hill, Jay-Z, Tupac, and Ice Cube as thinkers who probe God, love, authenticity, punishment, capitalism, and racial injustice. Like Socrates, the argument goes, the rap battle and frank street speech are cross-examination - philosophy done outside the academy.
017: Bob Dylan, the American singer-songwriter who reshaped popular music from the 1960s onward and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016, has written songs of protest, love, faith, and disillusion for six decades. His dense, allusive lyrics reward philosophical reading: essays trace an arc from Plato's ladder of love to Kierkegaardian despair, ask whether a racist killer is culpable or a 'pawn' manufactured by white supremacy, weigh the ethics of bootleg recordings, and test his protest politics against Kant's enlightenment and postmodern skepticism.
018: Harley-Davidson, the American motorcycle maker founded in 1903, builds the heavy, rumbling bikes that became icons of freedom and rebellion - Marlon Brando, Easy Rider, leather and bandanas. For riders a Harley is less a machine than a decision about how to live, which is exactly why it invites philosophy: essays use Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, Heidegger on authentic existence, the Hellenistic schools of ancient Greece, and Hegel and Marx to ask what the ride means, why bikers form an instant brotherhood, and how commerce corrodes it.
019: Monty Python was the British comedy troupe whose 1969-74 television show and films like Life of Brian and The Meaning of Life made surreal absurdity a pillar of popular comedy. The connection to philosophy is literal: several Pythons absorbed the linguistic analysis of Wittgenstein, Russell, and Ryle at Oxford and Cambridge in the 1960s. Essays use the Dead Parrot sketch to test theories of meaning, the Argument Clinic to illustrate Rawls, and Mr. Creosote to explain why we laugh at the monstrous - and ask whether comedy can answer life's absurdity.
020: Poker is the card game of betting and bluffing, and no-limit Texas Hold'em - the version played at the World Series of Poker - has made professionals like Doyle Brunson and Chris Ferguson celebrities, especially after television and the 2003 internet-qualifier boom. The game is a natural philosophy laboratory: every hand forces decisions under uncertainty, incomplete knowledge of other minds, and genuine risk. Essays weigh bluffing against Kantian honesty, read the all-in bet through Kierkegaard's leap of faith, and ask whether Dostoevsky was right that gambling exposes the limits of reason.
021: U2 is the Irish rock band - Bono, the Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. - that rose from late-1970s Dublin post-punk to become one of the world's biggest bands, with The Joshua Tree among rock's landmark albums. Their songs wrestle publicly with faith, love, fame, technology, and global suffering, which makes them fertile philosophical ground: essays read their longing songs through Plato's ladder of love, Bono's stage personas through Kierkegaard and Baudrillard, and the band's desert imagery through Heidegger on place and belonging.
022: Vampires and zombies are the Undead of popular horror - from Dracula and George Romero's zombie films to Twilight, True Blood, and Shaun of the Dead - and the twenty-first century has made them more popular than ever. They are also perfect thought experiments: is becoming a vampire worse than dying, does a zombie remain the person it used to be, and why do we kill zombies without qualms? Essays deploy Locke, Hume, Nietzsche, and the replicants of Blade Runner to interrogate personal identity, the badness of death, rights, and other minds.
023: James Bond is the British secret agent Ian Fleming created in 1953, known worldwide through the film series running since 1962 for its gadgets, glamour, and globe-trotting villains. Behind the martini and the license to kill lie serious questions: whether a hedonist can face death, what Plato's rulers would make of MI6, whether Bond is a Nietzschean overman or just a well-dressed animal, and how the rule of law survives a man who kills for queen and country.
024: In 2005, Princeton philosopher Harry Frankfurt's slim essay On Bullshit — a technical analysis of speechmakers who simply don't care whether what they say is true — unexpectedly spent months on the bestseller list. This book asks why that struck such a nerve, from the Iraq war's weapons claims to fabricated memoirs and product placement disguised as conversation. Its essays test, defend, and extend Frankfurt's definition, asking when bullshit is tolerable, how it differs from lying, and why philosophy itself may be our best defense against it.
025: The Beatles are the Liverpool quartet who became the most famous band in history, setting off Beatlemania in the 1960s and transforming popular music. This book treats their rise alongside Bob Dylan and Elvis Presley as a case study in how novelty enters culture: whether meaning is created rather than found, how the body's feelings drive what the mind thinks, whether Beatlemania was a genuine religious phenomenon, and how an artist's sense of destiny can make its own truth.
026: South Park is the gleefully vulgar animated satire that Comedy Central has run since 1997, following four Colorado boys through episodes that mock politicians, religions, and celebrities alike. The show was accused of corrupting the young for reasons strikingly like those that got Socrates executed. Its essays use Cartman, the Chewbacca Defense, and the theology of the show's over-the-top plots to teach logic, probe the problem of evil, question relativism, and ask why bad reasoning drives real laws and beliefs.
027: Alfred Hitchcock, the 'Master of Suspense' who directed from the 1920s to the 1970s, gave cinema Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window, and The Birds. His contributors argue the films are organized around ideas: Rope stages a botched Nietzschean superman's murder, Psycho poses the problem of horrendous evil, Shadow of a Doubt teaches the difference between belief and knowledge, and The Birds tests whether romantic love is worth its costs. Watching Hitchcock, we learn, means confronting how little we can know for certain.
028: The Grateful Dead were the San Francisco band at the heart of the 1960s counterculture, famous for never playing a song the same way twice and for a fan community, the Deadheads, that followed them from 1965 until Jerry Garcia's death in 1995. Their parking-lot markets, taping ethos, and Buddhist-tinged lyrics raise real questions: what makes a community, whether capitalism can care, who owns an improvised performance, and how a grinning skeleton became a guide to life and death.
029: Quentin Tarantino is the American director of Reservoir Dogs, Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill, and Death Proof, celebrated and criticized for stylized violence and endless talk about pop culture. His criminals argue about tipping, foot massages, and whether a bullet that missed was a miracle — and the films ask whether even hitmen live by a morality. Essays draw on Nietzsche, Hume, and Rawls to ask whether revenge can be justified, and whether watching it all is corrupted spectatorship or something deeper.
030: Pink Floyd, the English band formed in 1965, turned psychedelic experiment into monumental concept albums — The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals, The Wall — meditations on time, money, madness, and alienation. Their songs interrogate the schools that indoctrinate us, the markets and states of Animals' beast fable, and the industry that commodifies artists. Was founder Syd Barrett's madness the price of art, and was the band punk before punk existed?
031: Johnny Cash, the 'Man in Black,' was country music's great outlaw conscience, famous for prison concerts at Folsom and San Quentin, gospel hymns, and songs of murderers, drifters, and working men. He was also, as Kris Kristofferson said, a walking contradiction: an addict and a devout Christian. His songs ask what an authentic self is when the persona was manufactured, what makes work meaningful, what makes a law unjust, and how evil fits a world made by a benevolent God.
032: Bruce Springsteen, 'The Boss,' has since the 1970s been America's foremost rock chronicler of working-class life, from Born to Run to Born in the U.S.A. to The Rising. His songs of factories, failed promises, and hard-won hope raise questions philosophers usually save for books: whether he is a prophet or merely a poet, what Marx would make of his characters, whether encores are gifts or obligations, and how a flag-wrapped protest song can be a lesson in democracy.
033: Battlestar Galactica is Ronald D. Moore's acclaimed 2004-2009 reimagining of the 1978 space opera: humanity's last remnants flee genocidal Cylon robots, and the Cylons evolve into indistinguishable human copies. That premise is a philosophy engine. The essays ask what identity means when memories are fabricated (the two Sharons, Starbuck's recovered past), whether the self is a story we retell, and what forgiving genocide's collaborators requires. The book even includes five unattributed chapters, like the show's hidden Final Five.
034: Apple's iPod, launched in 2001, made a thousand songs pocketable and reshaped how a generation consumed music. This book treats it as a genuinely philosophical object: what does the private 'audio cocoon' do to our encounters with other people, and is the personified click wheel a symptom of Marx's reification? Essays range from Wittgenstein on why there's no essence of 'iPod' to the Foxconn labor behind the glossy shell, the trade-off between playlists and albums, and whether the solitary listener is freer or lonelier for it.
035: Star Trek, Gene Roddenberry's optimistic science-fiction franchise since 1966, sends starship crews into dilemmas that double as classic philosophy problems; its writers always smuggled in 'a heavy idea or two.' This volume mines the shows accordingly: 'Darmok' as Wittgenstein on language, Spock and Data's emotion debate as Stoics versus Aristotelians, Khan's vengeance through Nietzsche, Q's omnipotence through Plato's Ring of Gyges. Its title riffs on The Wrath of Khan, and its premise is that Trek's humanism is philosophy disguised as entertainment.
036: Nintendo's Legend of Zelda, running since 1986, is the beloved action-adventure series in which the hero Link explores Hyrule, solves dungeons, and rescues Princess Zelda. Because the player guides rather than watches, it raises questions most games barely touch: why do we feel real fear and sorrow for Wind Waker's cartoon characters, and what makes Hyrule a place when warping erases the journey? Essays bring Plato's Meno to the item-room fanfare, existentialism to Link's drudgery, and a meditation on death to switching the console off.
037: The Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel and the beloved 1939 film starring Judy Garland — follows Dorothy from gray Kansas over the rainbow to a land of witches, Munchkins, and companions seeking brain, heart, and courage. That simple quest carries serious philosophical freight. Essays stage Kant as Chancellor of Munchkinland to judge the Wizard's lies, read the journey through Hegel, trace the companions' virtues with Aristotle, and connect Baum's Kansas to the abolitionist history of Bleeding Kansas and John Brown.
038: Radiohead, the English band who followed 1997's OK Computer and 2000's Kid A from guitar rock into uneasy electronic soundscapes, are widely regarded as the most cerebral band of their era. This book asks why the music feels philosophical at all: its title takes Yorke's deadpan robot-voice track 'Fitter Happier' as emblem of a technology-saturated life. Essays use Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty on our immersion in machines, Marx on the pay-what-you-want In Rainbows release, and the 'All I Need' anti-trafficking video to show emotion doing argumentative work.
039: Jimmy Buffett, the singer-songwriter behind 'Margaritaville' and 'Cheeseburger in Paradise,' built a laid-back beach-escapist mythology and a devoted fanbase of 'Parrotheads.' This book takes his hedonism seriously as philosophy: Buffett appears as an Epicurean who knows pleasure needs prudence ('I know it's my own damn fault'), a Stoic controlling attitudes rather than circumstances, and a Heideggerian case that what we really escape is the weight of having to be at all. The title wryly sets his secular 'Porpoise Driven Life' against Rick Warren's Purpose Driven one.
040: Transformers, the Hasbro toy line turned 1980s cartoon and hit film franchise, follows warring alien robots — heroic Autobots led by Optimus Prime against Megatron's Decepticons — who disguise themselves as vehicles and machines. The premise is a philosophy goldmine: what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or truck, do these machines have minds, moral status, or souls, and would real First Contact be with AI explorers rather than biological aliens? As the editors note, probing Transformer nature ends up probing human nature, since they are our own creations.
041: Stephen Colbert's The Colbert Report (2005-2014) was a Peabody-winning satire in which he played a blowhard faux-pundit who 'feels the news at us,' coining 'truthiness' — truth by gut feeling — along the way. The character is a philosopher's dream and a philosopher's punching bag. Essays use him to dismantle relativism and the 'right to my opinion,' read his dueling Formidable Opponent segments as real moral deliberation, apply Grice and Russell to nonsense words like 'freem,' and ask whether his Platonic play teaches Americans something Puritanism never let them learn.
042: Comic-book supervillains — the Joker, Magneto, Lex Luthor, Doctor Doom, Watchmen's Ozymandias — have grown from mustache-twirlers into the most humanized characters in the medium, which is exactly why they deserve philosophy. This volume asks whether anyone can truly will evil, whether tyranny can serve a good cause, why henchmen always betray (Aristotle and Hobbes have answers), and whether Rorschach's unbending Kantianism beats Ozymandias's utilitarian massacre. Essays also test omnipotence with Galactus, personal identity with Venom, and whether Brainiac's disembodied 'pure logic' would actually make him dumber than us.
043: Philip Pullman's His Dark Materials trilogy, beginning with The Golden Compass (1995), is a celebrated fantasy series about the girl Lyra, her shape-shifting dæmon, and a journey across parallel worlds to overthrow 'the Authority' himself. The books are famously controversial for attacking organized religion, which makes them rich ground for philosophy: whether Pullman's god is really the God of the philosophers, whether lying and storytelling can be virtues, what the soul-splitting of children says about belief, and whether heresy corrupts young readers or teaches them to think.
044: Led Zeppelin, the English hard-rock band of the late 1960s and 1970s behind 'Stairway to Heaven' and 'Whole Lotta Love', were dismissed by critics as blues thieves and purveyors of mere excess, yet their occult imagery and myth-soaked lyrics were the work of serious spiritual seekers. Their music raises real philosophical questions: whether their thunderous sound is an experience of the sublime, how a band creates as a group, whether uncredited borrowings undermine their authenticity, and why their lyrics so often demean women.
045: World of Warcraft, Blizzard's massively multiplayer online game running since 2004, lets millions of players quest, raid, and trade in the fantasy world of Azeroth. The world is virtual but the people are real, and that gap generates genuine philosophy: is killing players at an in-game funeral murder or fair play, does the auction house model perfect market economics, can a game answer nihilism, and does a character controlled entirely from above have free will? The book itself is framed like a quest log.
046: Mr. Monk, the USA Network comedy-drama (2002-2009), stars Tony Shalhoub as Adrian Monk, a brilliant detective whose obsessive-compulsive disorder is both the 'gift and curse' behind his casework and the ruin of his daily life. The show is a goldmine for philosophy: Monk as Camus's happy Sisyphus in a war on dirt he can never win, his phenomenological way of seeing what the rest of us miss, whether his epiphanic certainty about whodunit is justified, and what his halting friendships reveal about Aristotle's virtues.
047: Anime, Japanese animation, ranges from the giant-robot violence of Akira and Neon Genesis Evangelion to the gentle spirits of My Neighbor Totoro, and it is emphatically not children's fare. Its shape-shifting bodies, cyborgs, and uploaded minds make it perhaps the richest medium for asking what a person is: is Motoko of Ghost in the Shell still herself when she merges with the net, is the monstrous Tetsuo of Akira still Tetsuo, and are we already cyborgs anyway? The book reads these stories through posthuman theory, gender, and tragedy.
048: The Boston Red Sox are baseball's great tragedy-to-triumph story: for eighty-six years after selling Babe Ruth to the Yankees, the team broke its fans' hearts in increasingly improbable ways, until the miracle 2004 championship changed everything. That history makes fandom itself a philosophical subject: how to govern the emotions a game provokes, what makes an authentic rather than bandwagon fan, whether losing teaches what winning cannot, and what the curse's end did to a community long glued together by shared doom.
049: The twenty-first century has seen a boom in the Undead, from Twilight and True Blood to zombie walks and Romero-style splatter films, and this book asks why these monsters in particular fascinate us. The vampire, a superhuman predator charged with guilt, and the zombie, dead flesh that shambles beyond all morality, let philosophers probe personal identity (would it be me rising?), whether Undeath could really be worse than death, whether the Undead can be evil, and what the philosophical-zombie thought experiment owes to its fictional namesakes.
050: Facebook, the social network launched in 2004, now shapes how billions of people friend, post, and perform their lives online, and this book takes that everyday apparatus seriously. Chapters ask whether trivial status updates can still matter, how the site breaks the old 'know your audience' rule of privacy, whether a Facebook friend is an Aristotelian friend, whether profiles foster authenticity or a surrogate self that mourns on our behalf, and whether users' unpaid posts amount to digital labor in a walled garden.
051: Soccer, the world's most popular sport, rests on one rule: move the ball into the net without using your hands. From that simplicity the book derives big questions: why a ball crossing an arbitrarily drawn line ignites passions on every continent, whether the 'best' team can really lose (and what that even means), how luck, injustice, and drama make the game a rehearsal for life, what Nietzsche would make of Arsenal, and why a beautiful goal might be a moral as well as an aesthetic achievement.
053: This book is not about one pop-culture work but about the world's fighting traditions - karate, kendo, judo, boxing, fencing, and the Shaolin Temple - which have always sat close to philosophy: Plato wrestled, and Zen shaped the samurai swordsmanship of writers like Takuan Soho. The essays ask what a black belt actually certifies, whether dojo courtesy could ever matter in a real fight, how a kendo master can strike without thinking, whether the self that martial training masters even exists, and what Buddhist no-self does for compassion in combat.
054: The Onion is the satirical newspaper famous for deadpan fake headlines like 'World Death Rate Holding Steady At 100 Percent' and 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer', read here alongside its syndicated advice columns. Its satire is philosophical on purpose: the essays treat ridicule as a tool for exposing self-deception, ask whether belief in God survives the evidence, probe the morality of swearing and of calling someone an asshole, and wonder whether every generation thinks the next one is dumber. Voltaire would recognize the project.
055: Doctor Who is the BBC's long-running science fiction series (since 1963) about the Doctor, a time-traveling alien who explores the universe in the TARDIS and, when mortally wounded, regenerates into a new body and personality. That regeneration gimmick alone raises hard questions about what makes someone the same person, and the show piles on more: time-travel paradoxes, whether the Daleks could count as people, what makes the Doctor's mercy special, and what his wonder-struck companions teach us about the love of wisdom.
056: Dune is Frank Herbert's 1965 science fiction epic, set on the desert planet Arrakis, where the young noble Paul Atreides gains messianic power over the Fremen and the spice that drives interstellar civilization. The essays wrestle with what Herbert built into the story: whether Paul's foreseen future leaves any room for freedom, the ethics of the Bene Gesserit's breeding programs and Leto II's tyrannical Golden Path, the test of what makes a human, war and empire, and a religion and ecology that read uncomfortably like our own politics.
057: Rush is the Canadian power trio of Geddy Lee, Alex Lifeson and Neil Peart, beloved since the 1970s for virtuosic, intricately structured rock with lyrics about science, individualism and dystopias, and just as famously polarizing among critics. The essays ask whether the band deserves its reputation as a 'thinking man's band': is complex rhythm really mind opposed to body, does Neil Peart owe anything to Ayn Rand, what makes a cover or a drum-along faithful, and what Rush's cult of craft says about taste, technique and authenticity.
058: Dexter is the Showtime drama (2006-2013) about Dexter Morgan, a Miami forensic technician who is also a serial killer, channeling his urges into murdering murderers under the strict rules his foster father called Harry's Code. That premise makes him a perfect laboratory for ethics: can a remorseless sociopath be decent or even praiseworthy, is he blameworthy for urges born of childhood trauma, does his 'be sure' rule ever amount to knowledge of guilt, and what do his emotionless life and vigilante justice reveal about what a good life requires?
059: Halo is the blockbuster Xbox science fiction game series launched in 2001, casting the player as Master Chief, a faceless super-soldier fighting the alien Covenant alongside the AI Cortana. The essays argue there is more going on than shooting aliens: which of a million players' Master Chiefs is the real one, whether Cortana could pass the Turing test, whether the Spartan program's child-soldiers live absurd or Stoic lives, whether Plato would count Halo as guardian training, and what a game owes us if it wants to count as art.
060: SpongeBob SquarePants is the Nickelodeon cartoon (since 1999) about an irrepressibly cheerful sea sponge who flips Krabby Patties in the underwater town of Bikini Bottom, adored by children and adults alike. The essays find real philosophy under the sea: SpongeBob as Aristotle's virtuous mean, the happy ignoramus Patrick measured against Mill's discontented Socrates, Squidward as Schopenhauer's suffering will, Mr. Krabs's money worship weighed against Marx and Adam Smith, Sandy Cheeks as feminist scientist, and what it takes to have the best day ever.
061: Sherlock Holmes is Arthur Conan Doyle's legendary consulting detective (from 1887), who solves apparently impossible cases from Baker Street by minute observation and startling inference, alongside his chronicler Dr. Watson. The essays treat the canon, and its screen Holmeses, as a philosophical quarry: are Holmes's deductions knowledge or luck, how does abduction actually work, is he Spinoza's free man or Nietzsche's self-fashioned overman, what makes his friendship with Watson the best kind, and does his method anticipate Heidegger?
062: Inception is Christopher Nolan's 2010 film about thieves who enter people's dreams to steal, and plant, ideas, ending on the spinning top that may or may not tell Cobb he is awake. The essays use it to dig into skepticism and the self: how do we know we are not dreaming, what is wrong with planting a thought in someone's mind, can our very thoughts be other than our own, does Nozick's experience machine explain why Cobb leaves Limbo, and is the happy ending a choice rather than a proof.
063: Philip K. Dick is the science fiction author whose paranoid novels and stories inspired Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report and The Adjustment Bureau, works where false memories, androids indistinguishable from people, and manipulated realities are the norm. The essays trace what Hollywood keeps losing in adaptation: Dick's dark vision of accepted unfreedom and permanent doubt against the silver screen's free will and happy endings, whether Deckard could be an android without any evidence settling it, and whether the ancient skeptics' tranquility is the only sane response.
064: The Rolling Stones are the British rock band behind 'Paint It, Black', 'Gimme Shelter', and 'Sympathy for the Devil', famous for their blues-rooted swagger and for still touring into their seventies. A band proud of its anti-intellectual image turns out to raise real philosophical questions: what a song or a band actually is when every performance changes it, whether genius can exist only in a partnership like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, what it means to keep searching for satisfaction, and how a devil's-eye view of evil holds up.
065: Chuck Klosterman is an American essayist whose 2000s books, such as Sex, Drugs, and Cocoa Puffs and Killing Yourself to Live, made a name for treating rock bands, sports, cereal, and sitcoms with lethal seriousness. His trademark question — whether 'guilty pleasures' make any sense, or whether nothing is ever just itself — invites philosophy at a busy intersection: Kant on perspective, Kierkegaard on irony, Nietzsche on masks, and honest puzzles about self-knowledge, tribute bands, and whether culture itself can be wrong.
066: Neil Gaiman is the British author of American Gods, Coraline, and The Sandman comics, beloved for fantasy in which ordinary people stumble into hidden worlds ruled by old stories. That premise is a philosopher's playground: gods who exist only because people believe in them raise questions about what belief and personhood are; con-men gods staging 'coincidences' test Hume on causation; Plato's case against poetry gets answered by Aristotle; and Gaiman's dream realm asks whether our nightly dreams might be visits to a real place.
067: Breaking Bad is the acclaimed AMC drama (2008-2013) in which Walter White, a high-school chemistry teacher with cancer, starts cooking methamphetamine and slowly becomes a monster. The show is a deliberate morality play in the line of Macbeth and Faust, and the questions follow naturally: what really drove Walt, how we should grade each of his killings, whether a strict materialist can have a soul, whether 'Heisenberg' is a lie or an authentic self, and what doctors and families owe a dying man's choices.
068: The Walking Dead is the hugely popular comic and AMC series about survivors of a zombie apocalypse, where law, government, and property are gone and the dead walk as mindless 'walkers'. The premise works as a philosophy laboratory: Hobbes's state of nature becomes a question about how survivors should treat each other, while the walkers themselves probe consciousness, personal identity, knowledge, and personhood — and force the uncomfortable question of whether killing a walker is murder or mercy.
069: Curb Your Enthusiasm is the long-running HBO sitcom in which Seinfeld co-creator Larry David plays a wealthy, tactless version of himself who says what everyone else suppresses. Because the show runs on unwritten social rules and what happens when one man ignores them, it invites philosophy from several directions: classic theories of humor, Heidegger and Wittgenstein on the background practices nobody notices, whether civility's rules can be justified, what Larry's devoted idleness is worth, and whether the Larry on screen is a character or the man.
070: Dungeons and Dragons, created by Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson in 1974, is the tabletop role-playing game where friends gather around dice and imagination to tell fantasy stories together. That setup turns out to be fertile philosophical ground: what kind of thing a game even is, whether playing is mere escapism or genuine art, whether playing an evil character convincingly refutes virtue ethics, how the nine-fold alignment system maps onto Kant and Mill, and why losing a beloved character can hurt like real grief.
072: Jeopardy! is America's most famous quiz show, running since 1964 on its signature gimmick: contestants are given answers and must phrase their responses as questions. A game built entirely on facts and wagers is surprisingly deep territory: what knowledge is and whether the judges own it, whether the game is genuinely fair or a portrait of American meritocracy, what makes a game good at all in Bernard Suits's sense, and what IBM's Watson victory over champions like Ken Jennings says about thinking machines.
073: The Wire is the HBO crime drama (2002-2008) that followed the police, drug dealers, dockworkers, politicians, schoolchildren, and journalists of Baltimore, and is widely regarded as one of television's great novels. Its sweep raises sweeping questions: how post-industrial capitalism quietly devalues whole neighborhoods, whether the drug trade's 'Game' traps everyone in a rigged cycle, what it means that some Americans live with rights only on paper, and whether a father's partiality or an impartial moral code better explains the show's best and worst moments.
074: Planet of the Apes began with the 1968 film in which astronaut Charlton Heston crash-lands on a world where articulate apes rule and mute humans are animals — and it continues today with the Rise prequels about the intelligent chimp Caesar. The reversal does real philosophical work: Taylor in the dock replays Galileo's trial, Zira's lab dissections echo Descartes's beast-machine doctrine, and the films press hard questions about other minds, whether language or deception is the true test of personhood, and the ethics of enhancing animals.
075: Psych is an American TV comedy-detective series (2006-2014) about Shawn Spencer, a private consultant so observant that he convinces the Santa Barbara police he is psychic. The show's running con raises real philosophical puzzles: when is lying justified if it catches killers, how can bad logic lead to true conclusions, and does Shawn's fluency in abduction, thin-slicing, and Gettier cases amount to knowledge? His hyper-observation turns every case into an epistemology lesson.
076: The Good Wife is an American legal drama (CBS, 2009-2016) about Alicia Florrick, who rebuilds a law career while standing by her politician husband after a prostitution scandal. Unlike older courtroom shows, it follows lawyers home, where compromises get personal. Its cases probe the ethics of zealous advocacy, drone warfare, utilitarian client-pleasing, Kantian duty versus an ethic of care, and what a woman owes her family, her lovers, and herself.
077: Boardwalk Empire is HBO's Prohibition-era crime drama (2010-2014), following Atlantic City treasurer and bootlegger Nucky Thompson through the world of Capone, Lucky Luciano, and corrupt G-men. A show about criminals who must lie, charm, and kill to hold power is naturally philosophical territory: the essays test Nucky against Machiavelli's Prince and Nietzsche's Superman, read Jimmy and Richard as veterans facing existential despair, and ask whether the docudrama itself misleads viewers about real history.
078: Futurama is Matt Groening and David X. Cohen's animated sci-fi comedy (first aired 1999-2003, later revived), following delivery-boy Fry, frozen in 1999 and awakened in the year 3000. Behind the jokes it is a serious science-fiction show, and the essays use its episodes to argue about free will and self-government, flag burning and tolerating offensive speech, ecological waste, the ethics of war, and why 'perversion' is an arbitrary judgment. The mundane made strange does real philosophical work.
079: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is the novel of a scientist who reanimates dead flesh and abandons his nameless creature, and its monster has since spread through hundreds of films, from Boris Karloff to Mel Brooks and Herman Munster. The story keeps earning philosophy because it condenses modern anxieties: is 'playing God' a real wrong, what do creators owe their creations, does the creature have a soul, and what does the 'Frankenfood' metaphor get right or wrong about biotechnology today?
080: Ender's Game is Orson Scott Card's 1985 science-fiction novel (filmed in 2013), in which gifted children are trained at a Battle School to fight an alien enemy, and child genius Ender unknowingly wipes out an entire species. The book's traps are philosophical: can an engineered childhood be justified, is Ender's empathy also his weapon, is he virtuous or a pawn of disciplinary power, and who bears responsibility when the game turns out to be xenocide?
081: How I Met Your Mother is an American sitcom (CBS, 2005-2014) framed as Ted telling his children the long, digressive story of how he met their mother. Its trick is making viewers love Barney, an appalling manipulator, and the essays take that seriously: why we empathize with fictional badness, whether Barney's 'be awesome instead' is a theory of emotion, if ethical egoism can survive the Bro Code, and how the show stages Sartrean bad faith and non-essentialist feminism through Robin.
082: Jurassic Park began as Michael Crichton's 1990 novel and became Spielberg's 1993 blockbuster: scientists clone dinosaurs for a theme park, and the park predictably collapses. Its heart is Malcolm's question, not 'could we' but 'should we', which the essays pursue through the ethics of de-extinction, whether frog-patched clones are really dinosaurs (a Ship of Theseus puzzle), what a botched 'intelligent design' suggests about designers, and whether Hammond's arrogance, not science itself, is the real villain.
083: This book is not about a single show but about the Devil as a pop-culture figure: Hellraiser's Pinhead, The Devil's Advocate, the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil', demonic video-game villains, and Halloween folklore. Belief in Satan, the essays argue, deserves the same scrutiny as any other belief. They test whether the scales of justice require a Hell, ask what our names for the Devil fix in how we see him, and trace prophecy, free will, and bad faith through his many screen appearances.
084: Leonard Cohen (1934-2016) was a Canadian poet and novelist who became a beloved singer-songwriter, famous for 'Hallelujah' and a gravelly voice musing on love, loss, and faith. Because his songs sit oddly between high poetry and popular music, they invite philosophical questions: does the divide between high and popular art even hold? The essays read him through Stoicism and Pyrrhonian skepticism, Camus and Kierkegaard, Judith Butler on masculinity, and Hume on whether he was, in fact, a good singer.
085: Homeland is the Showtime espionage thriller (2011-2020) about Carrie Mathison, a brilliant, bipolar CIA officer convinced that Nicholas Brody, a Marine rescued after years as a prisoner of war, has been turned by al-Qaeda. The show's mind games make it philosophy-ready: essays here ask whether the brainwashed Brody is still the same person, what his PTSD does to his identity, whether suicide can ever be justified, whether terrorists' morality needs God, and how Carrie's colluding roles of agent, patient, and lover can be reconciled.
086: Girls was Lena Dunham's HBO comedy-drama (2012-2017) about four self-absorbed twenty-something women muddling through work, sex, and friendship in Brooklyn, famous for making its heroine Hannah memorably unlikable. That rawness is why it earns a philosophy book: essays debate whether portraying degrading sex can be anti-feminist, why the show resists Adorno's culture industry when Friends did not, whether Adam's run across Brooklyn was truly heroic, and whether narcissists like Hannah and Jessa can live an examined, meaningful life.
087: Adventure Time is Cartoon Network's beloved animated series (2010-2018) following Finn the boy and Jake the shapeshifting dog through the surreal post-apocalyptic Land of Ooo, praised for sneaking surprisingly heavy ideas into a kids' cartoon. This book takes the show at its word: essays ask whether Finn's faith in magic over Princess Bubblegum's science stunts his moral growth, what makes Ice King a tragic figure rather than a villain, when Princess Bubblegum's parental rule over candy citizens is legitimate, and whether Simon's crown-borne self-sacrifice was heroic.
088: Justified was FX's crime drama (2010-2015) about Raylan Givens, an Old West-style US Marshal policing his own home turf of Harlan County, Kentucky, where coal poverty and crime run deep. Its pilot poses the book's driving question: when Raylan gives a hitman until sundown to leave town and then shoots him, is that justice or murder with a badge? Essays probe proactive policing and the war on drugs, Boyd Crowder's coal-country rebellion through Hegel, the show's racial casting patterns, coolness as a virtue, and whether Raylan ever really knows who done it.
089: Steve Jobs, co-founder of Apple, made computers, music players, phones, and animated films (through Pixar) central to modern life while being by many accounts petulant and cruel; this book neither canonizes nor demonizes him. Essays examine his famous 'reality distortion field' through the ethics of deception, ask whether a counterculture hippie capitalist is a contradiction, grade him against Plato's cardinal virtues, explore how Pixar films taught a generation to recognize personhood in non-humans, and ask whether American schools could ever produce an entrepreneurial mind like his.
090: Dracula is Bram Stoker's 1897 Gothic novel about the Transylvanian vampire who moves to London to feed on the living, the source of over a century of film adaptations and the archetype of the vampire itself. This book asks why we keep inviting the Count into our evenings: essays weigh whether eternal life would be a curse of endless boredom, map Kierkegaard's stages of life onto Harker, Mina, and Van Helsing, read the blood exchange through Plotinus, and ask why a monster who obeys no morality still cannot enter without an invitation.
091: It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia is FX's long-running dark sitcom (since 2005) about 'the Gang,' five vain, amoral bar owners whose schemes ruin everyone around them without a flicker of remorse. Their total badness makes them a strange philosophical laboratory: essays use the Gang's values to compare against Homer's heroes, test hedonism through Nozick's experience machine, ask whether Charlie's lucky guesses amount to knowledge in Gettier's sense, diagnose CharDee MacDennis through Freud's id, ego, and superego, and pin down what makes the McPoyle brothers genuinely creepy.
092: Orange Is the New Black is the Netflix ensemble drama (2013-2019), adapted from Piper Kerman's memoir, about a privileged white woman serving time in a federal women's prison and the far more precarious inmates around her. Prison makes it natural philosophy territory: essays apply Sartre's bad faith to guards and lovers, Bentham's panopticon and Foucault to life under surveillance, Nietzsche to Sophia Burset's transition, and critical scrutiny to the show's racial framing, while asking what prisoners owe each other and whether anyone at Litchfield is authentic.
093: Doctor Who is the BBC's science-fiction institution (since 1963) about the Doctor, a time-traveling alien who regenerates into a new body and face instead of dying, touring the universe in a police box bigger on the inside. This follow-up volume chases the show's signature puzzles: could Clara really exist as multiple scattered echoes, does the Doctor's drift from self-described coward to gun-toting hero track the War on Terror, is 'Am I a good man?' answerable across regenerations, and how the show's shifting, regenerating format makes it a metaphor for television itself.
094: Divergent is Veronica Roth's dystopian YA series (2011-2013) and film franchise set in a ruined Chicago where society is sorted into five virtue-based factions, until Tris Prior's 'Divergence' proves she cannot be filed under any single one. The setup is a working philosophy experiment: essays read the faction serums against medicating 'difficult' children, test Abnegation's selflessness through Buddhist practice and Nietzsche's slave morality, compare the controlling Bureau to the Tuskegee study, and argue, with the editor, that Tris retraces Plato's cave, discovering the faction life is a lie worth dying for.
095: Downton Abbey is the hugely popular British TV drama (2010-2015) about the Earl of Grantham's family and their servants in the early twentieth century, following the manor through war, scandal, and the slow erosion of the aristocracy. Its strict class order turns out to be fertile ground for philosophy: the meaning of work, whether manners are morality, when lying is justified, women's rights, disability, and whether a life like Carson's or a death like Sybil's can be made sense of at all.
096: Hannibal Lecter is the cultured psychiatrist and cannibal serial killer at the center of Thomas Harris's novels, five films including The Silence of the Lambs, and the TV series Hannibal. He fascinates because he is brilliant, polite, and monstrous at once, which raises uncomfortable questions: what exactly is wrong with eating people, can his killings be dressed up in ethical theories, why do we admire an aesthete of murder, and what does his empathy with Will Graham and Clarice Starling say about us.
097: The Walking Dead is the long-running AMC series (and comic) about survivors of a zombie apocalypse where everyone is already infected. With civilization gone, it becomes a pressure test for ethics: why be moral when survival pushes against it, whether Dale's Kantian principles or Shane's consequentialism fit the new world, how attempted communities like Woodbury and Terminus fail, whether Jenner's despair was right, and what Carol's transformations cost.
098: The Princess Bride is the beloved 1987 fairy-tale adventure film, drawn from William Goldman's novel, about the farmhand Westley, the princess Buttercup, the avenger Inigo, and a giant named Fezzik, complete with a Battle of Wits and Miracle Max. Beneath the jokes sits real philosophy: what makes a promise binding, whether men of action may lie, why revenge feels sweet, what 'inconceivable' actually means, and whether Westley's rhetoric or Vizzini's logic wins the day.
099: Louis C.K. is the American stand-up comedian whose specials and the FX series Louie turned confession into comedy, mining parenthood, boredom, sex, and mortality. His bits read like thought experiments: why everything's amazing and nobody's happy, whether you get to be bored, what the 'forever empty' of death does to us, when anger beats hatred, and whether Dr. Bigelow's advice about back pain and heartbreak is really Stoicism wearing a cardigan.
100: Batman and Superman are DC Comics' two oldest and most famous superheroes: the billionaire vigilante who strikes fear into Gotham's criminals and the invulnerable Kryptonian who stands for truth and hope. Pitting them against each other is really an argument about ideals - who should we try to be like? Their rivalry raises questions of philosophical anarchism, chivalric self-restraint, Nietzsche's overman, evolutionary fitness, and whether a god is what we actually need.
101: Discworld is Terry Pratchett's comic fantasy series of forty-one novels set on a flat world carried through space by four elephants and a turtle. The jokes carry surprising philosophical weight: golems as metaphors for the words society writes into our heads, a con artist running the post office, Lord Vetinari's friendly guide to tyranny, censorship in a city's first newspaper, witches and dwarfs negotiating identity, and what Sam Vimes's stubborn commonsense can teach professional philosophy.
102: Orphan Black is the BBC America thriller (2013-2017) in which con artist Sarah Manning discovers she is one of many clones - all played by Tatiana Maslany - monitored by a biotech corporation that owns their DNA. The premise drives hard questions: can a company legally or morally own people, what makes each clone a distinct self, are the clones harmed by being engineered to exist, what do Buddhist ideas and sisterhood offer them, and is Sarah responsible for what her makers built into her.
103: David Bowie was the English singer-songwriter (1947-2016) who reinvented himself across five decades, from Ziggy Stardust and the Thin White Duke to the late-career Blackstar, shaping glam rock, electronic music, and popular culture. The constant change was itself his philosophy: Sartrean self-creation, whether anything persists beneath the personas, the artifice of authenticity, Buddhist impermanence, deliberate nonsense in his lyrics, and what it means to make facing death into a final work of art.
104: Red Rising is Pierce Brown's science fiction series (beginning 2015) about Darrow, a miner bred for a color-coded caste system on Mars, who is surgically remade as a member of the ruling Gold elite to destroy the society from within. Its brutal world is a playground for big questions: social Darwinism masquerading as nature, what makes a person the same after total transformation, whether Darrow is a hero or just a subtler villain, and whether love or vengeance should fuel a revolution.
105: Game of Thrones, HBO's adaptation of George R. R. Martin's fantasy saga, enthralled the 2010s with its dynastic wars, political scheming, and willingness to kill off anyone. Its sprawling cast of flawed, morally compromised characters is a philosopher's playground: essays here ask whether Arya's revenge makes the show itself morally suspect, what Ned Stark's ruinous honor teaches about tragedy, where power really comes from, and how humor, disability, consent, and prophecy work in Westeros.
106: Peanuts is Charles Schulz's beloved comic strip, running from 1950 to 2000, about round-headed Charlie Brown, his beagle Snoopy, and a circle of children who talk like anxious adults. Beneath the jokes about kites and footballs lies real melancholy: essays here read the strip through existentialism, asking why Charlie's endless failures carry dignity, whether Linus's Great Pumpkin faith could ever be rational, what Lucy's cruelty owes to Kant, and how happiness, desire, and morality look from the sandbox.
107: Deadpool is Marvel's 'Merc with a Mouth,' a scarred, wisecracking, unkillable mercenary famous for cracking jokes about the comics, films, and audience watching him. His fourth-wall breaking makes him an unlikely philosopher: essays here ask whether stepping outside his own story is the examined life, whether an immortal can still find life worth living, what separates hero from villain from asshole, and how much violence and bad taste a character can carry and stay lovable.
109: Mr. Robot is the USA Network thriller (2015-2019) about Elliot Alderson, a brilliant, mentally fragile hacker drawn into fsociety's plot to erase the world's debt by destroying the financial giant E Corp. The show's blend of paranoia, technology, and political rage raises hard questions: essays here ask whether the hack was anarchist revolution or revenge, whether it can be justified by just war theory, what privacy means in a surveilled economy, and who really holds power in a world run by the grid.
111: The Man in the High Castle, Philip K. Dick's novel and Amazon's series adaptation, imagines an America that lost World War II and is partitioned between Nazi and Japanese rule. The setting forces viewers to think the unthinkable: essays here ask whether resisting fascism counts as terrorism, why we end up rooting for Nazi characters, how architecture and propaganda shape belief, what keeps alternative memory alive under totalitarianism, and how close that dark timeline really is to ours.
112: The Americans is the acclaimed FX spy drama (2013-2018) about two Soviet KGB officers living undercover in 1980s Washington as an ordinary married couple with American-born children. This book uses the show's central tension between marriage and politics to ask big questions about power: where the patriarchal family and the state came from, how husbands and wives struggle over money, work, and sex, what the classic social contract theorists got wrong about women and race, and how much has changed since 1960.
113: Jimi Hendrix (1942-1970) is widely held to be rock's greatest guitarist, transforming electric guitar in barely four years with records like Are You Experienced and his incendiary Woodstock rendition of the Star-Spangled Banner. Essays here treat his sound as serious thought: his burning guitar and feedback as Zen teaching, his antiwar noise as philosophy you feel in the body, his quest for freedom and love, whether his chaotic genius fits Kant's account of creativity, and how many 'Jimi' identities one life can hold.
114: American Horror Story is FX's horror anthology (since 2011), with each season recycling American nightmare material: haunted houses, asylums, witches, freak shows, slasher hotels. Beneath the gore the show worries about identity and survival: essays here ask what demonic possession threatens in personal identity, whether death in the Murder House is really a harm, whether conjoined twins are one person or two, how to keep hold of reality in a gaslighting world, and why America itself keeps producing these stories.
115: Iron Man and Captain America are Marvel's two flagship heroes, and their clash in the Civil War storyline over government registration of superhumans split fans down the middle. This book takes their quarrel seriously as a debate over American values: essays here ask who is the better hero and the better friend, whether Tony's failures or Steve's certainties embody virtue, whether humility is a moral achievement or herd instinct, and whether either man's answer to the freedom-versus-security dilemma can be right.
116: George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) is the defining dystopia: Big Brother watches everyone, Newspeak shrinks thought, and the Party rewrites history in Winston Smith's Oceania. Far from obsolete, it reads like tomorrow's news: essays here ask whether 'alternative facts' put us inside the novel already, why the proles never revolt, how media monopoly and weaponized language do the Party's work, whether the real enemies of freedom are states or corporations, and what kind of thinking could resist it.
118: Scott Adams is the cartoonist behind Dilbert, the syndicated comic strip about a hapless engineer and his pointy-haired boss that satirized office life for three decades, and the author of books on business, success, and fiction like God's Debris. In 2016 he staked his reputation on a 'Master Persuader' hypothesis explaining Donald Trump's appeal, turning him into a genuinely divisive public thinker. Here philosophers test his claims about persuasion, facts, bias, humor, and democracy, asking whether his theories survive scrutiny and what his comedy of work actually teaches.
119: Twin Peaks is David Lynch and Mark Frost's landmark television mystery, first aired in 1990 and revived in 2017, in which FBI Agent Dale Cooper investigates the murder of homecoming queen Laura Palmer in a Pacific Northwest logging town that is dreamlike, quirky, and haunted by an evil called BOB. Famous for refusing to explain its own imagery, the show invites philosophical work on self-knowledge, knowledge and justification, Kantian duty, Freudian desire, doppelgangers, and why asking 'but what does it mean?' may be exactly the wrong question.
120: Amy Schumer is an American stand-up comedian whose raunchy, feminist comedy reached a wide audience through her sketch series Inside Amy Schumer and the film Trainwreck. Her jokes about body image, sex, drinking, and celebrity culture often make herself the target, which raises real questions: who is the butt of a self-deprecating joke, is selfishness ever an argument, and can comedy do philosophy? This book reads her sketches, stand-up, and films through Nietzsche, Freud, Aristotle, and Socratic ignorance to find out.
121: The Twilight Zone is Rod Serling's classic anthology series (1959-1964), in which ordinary people encounter time loops, talking slot machines, robots, and wishes granted with malicious precision, all capped by a moral twist. It is beloved as the rare television show built entirely out of thought experiments. The essays here use its episodes to probe the nature of time, personal identity, whether a robot's love could be real love, why we trust faces, the ethics of lying, and the pleasure of the twist ending.
122: Westworld is HBO's science-fiction series (2016-) based on Michael Crichton's film, set in a western theme park where robotic 'hosts' are raped, murdered, and replayed daily by paying guests, until some of the hosts begin waking up and remembering. It is a hit built on one question: what happens to 'human' when machines suffer like us? Philosophers here take up consciousness, free will, simulation, memory and the self, and whether guests who torture sentient beings are monsters.
123: The Handmaid's Tale is Margaret Atwood's 1985 novel, now also a major television series, set in Gilead, a theocratic United States where fertile women are enslaved as 'Handmaids' to bear children for the ruling class. It endures because it reads less like fantasy than a catalog of things that have actually happened. The essays examine totalitarianism through Arendt, misogyny through Beauvoir and Genesis, language as a tool of control, Stoic resistance, and how close the present may be to Gilead's logic.
124: Tom Petty (1950-2017) was the Florida rock songwriter behind 'Free Fallin',' 'American Girl,' and 'I Won't Back Down,' a heartland Everyman whose band the Heartbreakers blended Byrds-style jangle with punk defiance across four decades. The essays argue his plainspoken songs reward philosophy: postmodern pastiche and the constructed 'real' Petty, MTV's inversion of music, trauma and repetition on the album Echo, Nietzschean self-creation, and a working musician's ethics of duty to fans against the record industry.
125: Rick and Morty is Adult Swim's animated sci-fi sitcom (2013-) about Rick, a nihilistic genius scientist, and Morty, his anxious grandson, whose portal-gun adventures across a multiverse of Dick pictures, Meeseeks, and microverse batteries made it a phenomenon. Under the gross-out humor lies a show about cosmic meaninglessness. The essays use Parfit on personal identity, Bostrom's simulation argument, the Euthyphro dilemma, and modal realism to ask whether anyone is really Rick, whether clones matter, and how to be happy anyway.
126: Stranger Things is Netflix's 1980s-set science-fiction horror series (2016-), in which kids on bikes in the town of Hawkins battle the Demogorgon and the Mind Flayer, monsters from the parallel 'Upside Down,' alongside the telekinetic girl Eleven. It is beloved for D&D friendship and Spielberg nostalgia, but it is also serious horror. The essays ask why we enjoy monsters, whether the Demogorgons deserve moral consideration, what Will's possession says about identity, and what the #JusticeForBarb phenomenon revealed about hyperreal justice.
127: Blade Runner 2049 is Denis Villeneuve's 2017 sequel to the 1982 sci-fi classic, following K, a replicant blade runner (bioengineered human) who hunts older models, discovers a replicant child, and questions whether his own memories are implanted. Its rain-slick, holographic Los Angeles is a staging ground for questions of personhood: can an AI companion like Joi love, what makes a life 'real,' do designer babies belong to their makers, and can Stoic self-cultivation make a manufactured being genuinely human?
128: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood was Fred Rogers's gentle PBS children's show, running from 1968 to 2001, that mixed puppets, Make-Believe, and unhurried talk about feelings. This book argues the show was quietly doing philosophy: Rogers took children's wonder seriously, asked Socratic questions about who we are, and insisted every person is lovable just as they are. Essays trace his kinship with Plato, Aristotle, and Daoist thought, and probe what his puppets, silences, and 'posthuman' neighbors say about personhood, play, and community.
129: RuPaul's Drag Race is the Emmy-winning reality competition, running since 2009, in which drag queens battle through challenges and lip syncs until RuPaul crowns the next drag superstar. It is also a rich philosophical playground: what makes a good queen, and is fierceness a virtue? Essays bring Aristotle to the judging panel, speech-act theory to reading versus shade, Baudrillard to 'realness', and game theory to the All Stars elimination twist, while asking how gender, self-love, and authenticity get performed in the werkroom.
130: The Good Place was the NBC comedy (2016-2020) in which self-absorbed Eleanor Shellstrop wakes in a heaven she was never meant for, tutored by the indecisive ethics professor Chidi Anagonye. Unusually for a sitcom, philosophy is the show's actual vocabulary rather than a gag. Essays weigh its afterlife point system against Kant, Arendt, and Nietzsche, ask whether anyone can ever do enough good to deserve paradise, puzzle over the trolley problem and Chidi's indecision, and take seriously the question of whether hell is other people.
131: The Infinity Saga is Marvel Studios' interconnected run of superhero films that climaxed in Avengers: Infinity War and Endgame (2018-2019), when the titan Thanos wiped out half of all life with a snap of his fingers. A villain with a coherent argument invites hard questions. Was Thanos a consistent utilitarian? Do the Avengers' time-travel fixes gamble with other people's rights? Essays on grief, sacrifice, population ethics, and Tony Stark's final choice treat the blockbusters as serious tests of moral theory.
133: Perry Mason, the courtroom drama starring Raymond Burr that ran from 1957 to 1966, adapted Erle Stanley Gardner's novels about a defense attorney whose clients are always innocent and whose cases always crack open in court. That tidy formula hides hard questions: was Mason actually good, or just lucky? Essays use moral luck and Kant to interrogate his record, compare him with Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, weigh perjury against reasonable doubt, and draw on psychology to show why eyewitness testimony so often fails.
134: KISS is the American rock band, famous since the mid-1970s for face paint, pyrotechnics, anthems, and the personas of the Demon, Starchild, Space Ace, and Catman. Beneath the spectacle the contributors find a workable philosophy: a steady message of self-belief and perseverance, Paul Stanley's hard-won examined life, and career bets made on Jamesian pragmatic faith rather than evidence. Essays also press the Ship of Theseus problem on a band that kept touring after its original members left, debunk the 'Knights in Satan's Service' rumor, and revisit KISS's disco detour.
136: 30 Rock was Tina Fey's Emmy-winning NBC sitcom (2006-2013) about Liz Lemon, the harried head writer of a live sketch show, her corporate overlord Jack Donaghy, and the uncontrollable star Tracy Jordan. The book treats the writers' room as a philosophy seminar: Aristotle's three friendships illuminate Liz and Jack's odd alliance, Marx explains Liz's alienated workaholism, Confucius indicts the show's settled-for 'semi-virtue', and Appiah and Fanon frame Tracy's performance of race. Even Kenneth the page's rule-worship gets its own ethical audit.
137: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is Lewis Carroll's 1865 classic - continued in Through the Looking-Glass and beloved through Disney's adaptation - about a girl who falls down a rabbit-hole into a world of grinning cats, mad tea parties, and backwards logic. Carroll was a logician, and the nonsense is rigorous. Essays read Alice's trial through Hobbes and Locke on consent and authority, the Mad Tea Party as Cold War deterrence strategy, the White Queen's jam rule as a problem of procrastination, and Wonderland's word games as lessons in how language can deceive.
138: Alien began with Ridley Scott's 1979 masterpiece - a haunted-house horror film in space, with Sigourney Weaver's Ripley battling an almost perfect killing machine - and grew into a franchise of sequels, prequels, and androids. Its bleak corporate future is philosophically loaded. Are Ash, Bishop, and David persons or property? What does Weyland-Yutani owe the crews it marks expendable? Essays on moral status, Marx, care ethics, and cosmic horror find the Xenomorph saga says as much about us as about the monster.
139: Arrested Development is the acclaimed sitcom (2003-2006, later revived by Netflix) about the Bluths, a wealthy, wildly self-absorbed family whose patriarch's fraud leaves level-headed Michael to hold them together, alongside Gob's failed illusions, Tobias's obliviousness, and Buster's mother fixation. The family's serial self-deception is philosophical gold. Essays test Socrates' claim that the examined life is happiest - and find the Bluths thriving without it - read Gob through Sartre's bad faith and Buster through Freud, and ask what, exactly, makes George Michael's kiss with his cousin wrong.
140: Avatar: The Last Airbender is a beloved Nickelodeon animated series (2005-2008) about Aang, a reluctant twelve-year-old savior who must master the four elements to end a century of imperial war. Its mix of Asian and Indigenous traditions, morally complicated villains, and a hero who refuses to kill gives it unusual depth for a children's show. This book asks what the series teaches about oneness, interdependence, chosen-one tropes, martial ethics, and whether nations themselves are illusions.
141: Avatar: The Last Airbender, Nickelodeon's acclaimed animated epic (2005-2008), follows Aang and his friends as they resist the Fire Nation's conquest in a world where people bend the four elements. The show's writers deliberately tested their characters' beliefs against their humanity, and its themes of genocide, imperialism, and the 'illusion of separation' invite serious thought. Essays here explore identity, disability, trust, and what a Chosen One story becomes when saving the world is a team effort.
142: The Avengers are Marvel Comics' flagship superhero team, famous since 1963 for pairing gods, soldiers, and geniuses with endless interpersonal drama. Because the team keeps quarreling over principle as much as villainy, it is rich material for philosophy. Chapters ask whether Iron Man, Captain America, and Thor embody utilitarian, deontologist, and virtue ethics; whether reformed villains deserve forgiveness; who counts as the real Captain America; and whether an android can truly love.
143: Batman, DC Comics' brooding vigilante, has fought Gotham's rogues gallery since 1939, and no hero's code invites harder questions. The essays here ask why Batman will not simply kill the Joker, whether it was right to recruit children as Robin, if a madman like the Joker can be held responsible at all, and whether Batman's existence exposes the failure of the state itself. His obsession, hatred, and discipline make him a philosophical case study, not just a hero.
144: Battlestar Galactica was the Syfy channel's acclaimed reimagining (2004-2009) of a 1978 space opera: the last remnants of humanity flee genocidal Cylons, machines that now look and feel human. The show was famous for taking on war, torture, abortion, and insurgency without flinching. Its questions run deep: if your memories and body betray you, who are you; can humans and their destroyers ever become one people; and what does our own history repeat when 'all of this has happened before'?
145: The Big Bang Theory was one of American television's most popular sitcoms (CBS, 2007-2019), following four brilliant but socially awkward scientists and the neighbor who humanizes them. Its running joke, that genius is no substitute for wisdom, is genuinely philosophical territory. Chapters weigh Sheldon's life of pure thought against Aristotle's ideal of flourishing, test the roommate agreement against Hobbes, probe the ethics of laughing at Sheldon's autistic-coded traits, and ask whether the gang's friendships are real at all.
146: The Big Lebowski is the Coen brothers' 1998 cult comedy about the Dude, an unemployed Los Angeles slacker mistaken for a millionaire and drawn into a kidnapping plot over a soiled rug. A box-office flop that became a way of life for its fans, it is quietly serious about how to live. Essays set the Dude's pacifist 'abiding' against Aristotle, Epicurus, and nihilism, asking whether his leisure is wisdom or waste, and what his friendships are really worth.
147: BioShock is a landmark video game series (2007 onward) set in failed utopias: the underwater city of Rapture, built on Ayn Rand-style objectivism, and the flying city of Columbia, built on American exceptionalism. Famous for its 'would you kindly' twist, which revealed the player's own choices were scripted, it turns games into philosophy. Chapters examine free will, whether the game fairly critiques Rand, Elizabeth's feminist liberation, and what ghosts and plasmids say about minds and bodies.
148: Black Mirror is Charlie Brooker's acclaimed British anthology series (2011 onward) of standalone near-future dramas about technology and its discontents, from social-media ratings to digital resurrection of the dead. Each episode works like a philosophical thought experiment rather than a simple gadget warning. Essays here ask whether coercion for the greater good is ever justified, what total transparency does to trust, whether a copy of your dead lover is your lover, and what justice really means when punishment becomes entertainment.
149: Black Panther (2018) made Marvel Comics' first Black superhero, created in 1966, into a cultural phenomenon: T'Challa, king of Wakanda, a secretly ultra-advanced African nation, torn between isolation and the world's oppressed. The film became a rare mainstream arena for debates about colonialism, reparations, and Afrofuturism. Chapters pit T'Challa's liberal internationalism against Killmonger's Pan-Africanism, weigh Wakanda's debts to the diaspora, and ask what African philosophy itself would have Wakanda offer the world.
150: Black Sabbath, formed in postwar industrial Birmingham in 1968, are widely credited with inventing heavy metal: slow, downtuned riffs, occult imagery, and Ozzy Osbourne's wail over songs about war, paranoia, and the end of the world. Accused of Satanism in their early years, they more plausibly wrote about real horrors, from nuclear annihilation to heroin. This book asks what actually makes their sound feel evil, whether their lyrics amount to an accidental philosophy of despair, and how Nietzsche, Camus, and Schopenhauer illuminate the doom they put on record.
152: The Daily Show, Jon Stewart's fake news program on Comedy Central from 1999 to 2015, became an unlikely source of political seriousness for a generation that got its news from comedy. By playing actual news footage straight and then puncturing it, the show forced questions about what television journalism had itself become. The essays here ask how a self-described fake newscast can inform viewers, whether mockery is a legitimate political voice, and what Baudrillard and Postman make of a media world where simulation and reporting blur.
153: Disney is less a single film than a universe: ninety years of animated classics, Pixar, theme parks, and the modern princess. This book treats that universe as a shared cultural vocabulary worth taking seriously. The essays range from Ariel's traded voice and the male gaze, through Mulan colliding with Confucian ideas of the self, to whether Hidden Mickeys hidden in the parks say anything about God, whether Inside Out gets emotions right, and whether the studio's happy endings are wisdom or calibrated escapism.
154: Doctor Strange began as a 1963 Stan Lee and Steve Ditko comic about an arrogant surgeon turned sorcerer, and reached a mass audience with the 2016 film starring Benedict Cumberbatch. His story, a scientist forced by catastrophe to accept magic, is a natural bridge between two ways of seeing the world. The essays read his crash and convalescence through Nietzsche and Heidegger, his famous 'I've come to bargain' time loop as the eternal return weaponized, and his comic-book trials as a working-out of Descartes' Meditations.
155: Downton Abbey, the ITV drama that ran from 2010 to 2015, follows an aristocratic family and their servants through the decline of the English country house in the early twentieth century. Its quiet domestic plots turn out to be dense with moral and social philosophy. The essays ask what makes work meaningful when nobody chooses their station, whether manners are ethics or their disguise, how money corrupts Matthew Crawley's romance, and why viewers raised on equality find the upstairs-downstairs hierarchy so fascinating.
156: Frank Herbert's Dune, published in 1965, is the best-selling science fiction novel of all time: a desert-planet epic of prophecy, ecology, and a chosen leader whose victory sets off a galactic holy war. Herbert's warning against heroes gives the book unusual philosophical depth. The essays take on Paul's paradoxical foreknowledge, the Bene Gesserit's eugenics programs, Leto II's tyrannical Golden Path, whether the Fremen are quintessentially American, and what Clausewitz and Habermas would make of the jihad Paul could not stop.
157: Dungeons and Dragons, the tabletop role-playing game Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson published in 1974, lets a group of friends build stories together around dice, rules, and improvised characters. Its forty-year lifespan has made it the standard case for what a game can be. The essays ask whether dungeon-crawling is mere escapism or Aristotelian art, whether playing an evil character teaches virtue or corrodes it, how the alignment system maps onto Kant and Mill, and whether grief over a character's death is rational.
158: Orson Scott Card's 1985 novel Ender's Game follows a gifted child trained through increasingly brutal war games to command humanity's fleet against an alien enemy, only to learn the final game was real. It is a staple of both military reading lists and school curricula, and its premise raises hard questions on purpose. The essays examine Battle School as Plato's Republic, Foucault's Panopticon, and a Freirean nightmare; ask whether Ender is responsible for xenocide he was tricked into; and trace how empathy becomes a weapon.
159: The Expanse, a novel series by James S. A. Corey adapted into a television run from 2015 to 2022, is hard science fiction about a colonized solar system split between Earth, Mars, and the exploited Belters of the asteroid belt, all destabilized by an alien technology. It is prized for taking politics, class, and physics seriously. The essays weigh who is more evil, Amos or Avasarala, whether humanity should risk extinction opening the Ring gates, and what Pascal and Kant make of its terrifying, beautiful infinite space.
160: Fallout is a long-running video game series, begun in 1997, set in an America devastated by nuclear war and steeped in 1950s retro-futurism, where players roam the wasteland making faction-defining moral choices. Its vault experiments and mutant underclass are designed as ethical sandboxes.
